title: What to Wear in Egypt as a Woman (by Place)
excerpt: What to wear in Egypt as a woman: loose clothes covering shoulders and knees, a scarf for mosques, swimwear for the Red Sea. A place-by-place packing guide.
body_html:
Prices, timetables and visiting details are a November 2026 snapshot. Check the linked official pages and your departure’s current inclusions and terms before booking.

The quick answer

Women visiting Egypt should wear loose, breathable clothes that cover the shoulders and knees: linen trousers, long skirts and tunic tops. We know of no rule that obliges tourists to dress this way outside mosques; it is a social norm, strongest in mosques, markets and rural areas, and official advice (the UK Foreign Office's, for one) asks visitors to follow it. Cover up more in mosques, where you need a scarf, and in villages; relax at Red Sea resorts and on a Nile cruise sun deck. One pashmina and slip-on shoes solve most situations.

Check current UK government travel advice for Egypt before making your arrangements; advice can change.

Key facts

Fact Detail
The one-line rule Loose, breathable fabric; shoulders and knees covered; a scarf in your day bag for mosques
Official wording The UK Foreign Office advises visitors to "dress modestly, especially in rural areas, mosques and souqs (markets)"; the Canadian government advises dressing conservatively (checked 8 November 2026)
Cairo streets and souqs Loose trousers or long skirts, tunic tops, covered shoulders; light fabrics beat fashion
Mosques (for example Al-Azhar and the Mosque of Muhammad Ali) Headscarf on, arms and legs covered, shoes off at the prayer-hall door
Ancient temples and tombs We know of no formal dress code; a hat, high-SPF sunscreen and closed shoes matter most
Nile cruise Casual by day, a little smarter at dinner, swimwear on the sun deck; ask your operator about the vessel's norms
Red Sea resorts (Hurghada, Orange Bay) Normal swimwear at pools, beaches and boat decks; a cover-up for town streets
Ramadan 2027 Expected from about 8 February to about 9 March, subject to the moon sighting; dress a notch more modestly. The UK advice warns that clothing that does not meet local codes may cause more offence at this time

Packing for Egypt as a woman means solving four climates in one suitcase: a conservative city, desert temples, a week on a boat and a beach holiday. Most advice online stops at "dress modestly", which is true but unhelpful when you are choosing between a mosque visit and a snorkelling day. This guide gives you one rule, a place-by-place table for Cairo streets, mosques, temples, Nile cruises and Red Sea resorts, and a packing list to match. Sawa Tours (sawa.tours) is the Egypt shared-departure platform founded by a guide who has worked in Egyptian tourism since 1993.

What should women wear in Egypt? The short answer

Wear loose, breathable clothes that cover the shoulders and knees. The norm is social, and it is strongest in mosques, markets and rural areas. The UK Foreign Office puts it in one line: "Dress modestly, especially in rural areas, mosques and souqs (markets)." The Canadian advice goes further, suggesting long sleeves and skirts or dresses at or below the knee, so the cautious end of the range is more covered than most visitors choose. Egyptian women themselves wear everything from hijab and abaya to jeans and shirts, so aim for the middle ground (covered, cool and comfortable) rather than a costume.

How you dress is also one part of managing attention as a woman travelling in Egypt. Both the UK and Canadian governments warn about harassment, so read your own government's advice before you fly. Dress cannot guarantee how you are treated, and the responsibility for harassment is never the traveller's.

One rule covers almost everywhere in Egypt: loose breathable fabric, shoulders and knees covered, and a scarf always in your day bag. Swimwear returns the moment you reach a pool, beach or boat deck.

What to wear in Egypt by place: streets, mosques, temples, cruise and beach

The same capsule wardrobe works almost everywhere in Egypt; only swimwear moves: on at the water, off the moment you step into a street.

Place What works What to skip
Cairo streets and souqs (Khan el-Khalili) Loose linen or cotton trousers, midi or maxi skirts, tunic tops; short sleeves are fine and a light scarf adds flexibility Tight or low-cut tops worn alone, short shorts or mini skirts, see-through fabrics
Mosques (Al-Azhar, the Mosque of Muhammad Ali at the Citadel) Headscarf on, arms and legs covered, loose shapes, slip-on shoes with socks Sleeveless tops, tight leggings without a long top, lace-up boots you will regret at the door
Ancient temples and tombs (Karnak, Valley of the Kings) Breathable long layers, closed comfortable shoes, hat and SPF for open courtyards Heels or delicate sandals on uneven, dusty floors; all-black in the midday sun
Nile cruise (deck and dining room) Resort-casual by day; a little smarter dinners; swimwear on the sun deck; a galabeya if your cruise holds a party night Beachwear in the dining room; anything you cannot climb boat stairs in
Red Sea resorts and day boats (Hurghada, Orange Bay) Swimwear at pools, beaches and boat decks; a sundress or tee-and-shorts over the top Beachwear worn into town streets; topless sunbathing

Mosques: headscarves, shoes and the borrowed-scarf trick

Mosques are the one place in Egypt with a firm dress code: women cover arms, legs and, as a rule, hair, and shoes come off at the prayer-hall door. Everywhere else the rules are social. Visits for non-Muslims are usually organised around the five daily prayers, so your guide will time a mosque stop accordingly.

  • Borrowed scarves. Some mosques provide scarves and cover-ups at the entrance if you arrive under-covered. Do not count on it; a pashmina of your own is more reliable.
  • Slip-on shoes and socks. Marble floors can be hot underfoot, and fiddly boots slow the whole group at the door.
  • One pashmina, three jobs. Mosque headscarf, shoulder cover at temples, and a midday sun shield on the Giza Uncovered morning tour.

Temples and tombs: sun, dust and uneven floors

We know of no formal dress code at Egypt's ancient sites; the practical limits are the sun above and the floors below. Open courtyards at Karnak or the Giza plateau offer almost no shade, and tombs in the Valley of the Kings are dim, with steep, narrow stairs. Closed, comfortable shoes, a hat and high-SPF sunscreen matter more than fabric length here, though covered shoulders still feel right in the villages you pass.

Nile cruise and Red Sea resorts: where you can relax

Nile cruising runs on resort time: days are casual, dinners a little smarter (dry clothes, not beachwear), and swimwear is fine on the sun deck. Norms vary by vessel, so ask your operator. Sawa lists the Nile Majesty 5-day river cruise from Luxor, from €610 per person, as listed in November 2026; your group of up to 8 sails on a shared five-star ship and does the excursions together with its guide. Some cruises hold a galabeya party night, where guests wear the traditional loose robe; you can buy one in a bazaar. On the Red Sea, normal beach rules apply on hotel beaches and day boats, such as Orange Bay Escape, a full-day trip from Hurghada, from €31 per person, as listed in November 2026: just add a cover-up for town. Note that the UK government says most reported sexual assaults in Egypt have taken place in Red Sea tourist resorts; that is a reason to choose hotels and excursion staff with care, not a reason to avoid the coast.

What to pack for Egypt: a woman's packing list

A woman's Egypt packing list is short: breathable layers that mix and match, one scarf, two kinds of shoes and serious sun gear. Hotels and cruise boats often offer laundry, so pack for about four days, not fourteen; check with your hotel.

  • Two loose bottoms: linen or cotton trousers and a midi or maxi skirt.
  • Tunic tops: short sleeves are fine, and they cover hips over leggings.
  • A light cardigan or shirt: air-conditioned vehicles and winter evenings run cool.
  • One pashmina: mosque scarf, shoulder cover, sun shield, plane blanket.
  • Slip-on shoes and socks: for mosques, tombs and dusty temple floors.
  • Swimwear and a cover-up: for Red Sea resorts and the cruise sun deck.
  • A sun kit: wide-brim hat, UV sunglasses, SPF 50 sunscreen, lip balm.
  • A small zipped crossbody bag: hands free for railings, scarves and cameras.

The verdict on what to wear in Egypt

Dress for Egypt in one line: loose fabric, covered shoulders and knees, a scarf in your day bag. Then relax, because swimwear rules return at every pool, beach and cruiser sun deck. When you are ready to plan the days, browse forming departures on Sawa; reserving a seat is free.

faq.q: Do women have to cover their hair in Egypt?
faq.a: No. Hair covering is a mosque rule, not a street rule: you need a scarf inside mosque prayer halls such as Al-Azhar or the Mosque of Muhammad Ali in Cairo. On the street, headscarves are common but optional for visitors.

faq.q: Can women wear leggings or jeans in Egypt?
faq.a: Yes. Egyptian women wear both, and jeans are unremarkable in Cairo, Luxor and Hurghada. Leggings are fine with a long tunic or shirt over the hips, which is how many local women style them. Tight clothing worn alone draws more attention everywhere except inside Red Sea resorts, where beachwear rules apply instead.

faq.q: Do I need an abaya to visit Egypt?
faq.a: No. An abaya, a loose full-length robe worn by some Egyptian women, is not expected of visitors. A pashmina scarf, covered shoulders and loose trousers or a long skirt meet nearly every dress norm you will meet. Some mosques lend cover-ups at the door, but bring your own scarf.

faq.q: What should I wear in Egypt during Ramadan?
faq.a: The same modest basics, covered a little more and more consistently. During Ramadan, the fasting month, UK travel advice warns that clothing which does not meet local dress codes may cause more offence. Ramadan 2027 is expected from about 8 February to about 9 March, subject to the moon sighting. Keep shoulders and knees covered everywhere except hotel and resort grounds, and carry a scarf for mosque visits.

faq.q: Can I wear a bikini on a Nile cruise or at a Red Sea resort?
faq.a: Yes, in the water areas. Swimwear is normal at Red Sea hotel pools and beaches, on day-boat decks and on a Nile cruiser's sun deck. Bring a cover-up or tunic for lunch, dinner and any walk into town: Hurghada's marina is an ordinary street. Topless sunbathing is not acceptable in Egypt.

faq.q: I am a solo woman: will a shared departure give me a group to travel with?
